title: The history of understanding the intestines
tagline: 4,000 years from Egypt's 'shepherd of the anus' to swallowable cameras, a gut surface the size of a small flat, and a drink of salt, sugar and water that has saved millions of children.
intro: For most of history people knew food went in one end and waste came out the other, but not what happened in between. Ancient doctors thought food was cooked in the stomach and turned into blood by the liver. Slowly, by cutting, looking through lenses, swallowing things and taking X-rays, people found a long, folded tube that squeezes food along, breaks it down with juices, soaks it up through millions of tiny fingers and shares the job with trillions of bacteria. Knowing how the gut soaks up salt and sugar led to one of the simplest life-savers in medicine.

eras.name: Cooking and channels
eras.summary: Egyptian doctors treat the bowels as blocked channels, and Galen teaches that food is cooked in the stomach and turned into blood by the liver. His ideas rule for well over a thousand years.

eras.name: Looking inside
eras.summary: Anatomists cut, look and draw for themselves. They find milky vessels for fat, folds, glands, patches and tiny pits in the gut wall, many still named after them.

eras.name: Juices and experiments
eras.summary: Scientists swallow bags of food, study a man with a hole in his stomach, and show that digestion is chemistry done by juices, with the pancreas as the great fat-breaker.

eras.name: Squeezes and signals
eras.summary: X-rays reveal the gut's waves of squeezing, the first hormone is found in the intestine, and doctors learn that gluten and too little fibre can make the gut sick.

eras.name: Salt, sugar and water
eras.summary: Knowing how the gut pulls in sodium and glucose together leads to oral rehydration salts, first proved in Bangladesh and India, and then used to save millions of children worldwide.

eras.name: The world inside
eras.summary: From yogurt bacteria to genome sequencing, people discover that the gut is home to trillions of microbes, and new tools measure and film the gut as never before.

events.title: Shepherds of the anus
events.text: Egypt had doctors who looked after the bowels, with a title that meant 'shepherd of the anus', recorded from around 2200 BCE. The Ebers Papyrus, from about 1550 BCE, lists remedies for constipation and other gut troubles. Egyptian doctors thought illness came from blocked channels inside the body, a bit like a blocked river, so they used laxatives and enemas to clear them.
events.why: It is some of the oldest written evidence of people trying to understand and treat the gut.

events.title: Food is cooked, then turned into blood
events.text: Galen, a Greek doctor in the Roman Empire, taught that food is 'concocted', a kind of cooking, in the stomach into a juice called chyle. He said veins in the gut wall soak up the chyle and the portal vein carries it to the liver, which turns it into blood. His books were followed for well over a thousand years.
events.why: He was right that the gut's blood goes straight to the liver, and his model shaped every later question about digestion.

events.title: An anatomy book that looked for itself
events.text: Vesalius, a young Flemish professor, dissected human bodies himself and published a huge illustrated book, De humani corporis fabrica. It showed the stomach, intestines and the rest of the body drawn from real dissections. Where Galen had described animals, Vesalius pointed out the differences in humans.
events.why: It taught doctors to trust what they could see over what old books said.

events.title: Milky vessels that carry fat
events.text: Aselli opened a dog that had just eaten and saw white threads on its intestines that oozed a milky liquid. He named them lacteals, milky veins. His book about them came out in 1627, two years after he died, with some of the first anatomy pictures ever printed in colour.
events.why: Lacteals are how the gut absorbs fat, and they were the first part of the lymph system to be found.

events.title: Folds that make the gut bigger inside
events.text: Kerckring, a Dutch doctor, described the ring-shaped folds that line the inside of the small intestine in his atlas, Spicilegium anatomicum. They are still sometimes called the valves of Kerckring. Today they are known as circular folds.
events.why: The folds are the first of three layers of folding that give the gut a huge surface for soaking up food.

events.title: Patches in the gut wall
events.text: Peyer, a Swiss doctor, described clusters of little lumps in the wall of the small intestine. He thought they were glands. We now call them Peyer's patches and know they are part of the immune system.
events.why: They are guard posts where the body checks what is passing through the gut.

events.title: Glands that protect the duodenum
events.text: Brunner, a Swiss anatomist, described glands in the wall of the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine, now called Brunner's glands. They make a slippery, alkaline mucus. A few years earlier, in 1683, he had removed a dog's pancreas and seen it become very thirsty, an early clue to diabetes.
events.why: The mucus helps protect the gut from the acid that arrives from the stomach.

events.title: Tiny fingers and pits
events.text: Lieberkühn, a German anatomist, filled blood vessels with coloured wax and studied the gut under the microscope. His book described the villi, tiny finger-like bumps, in great detail, and the small pits between them, now called the crypts of Lieberkühn. The crypts are where new gut lining cells are made.
events.why: Villi and crypts are the heart of how the small intestine absorbs food and renews itself.

events.title: Swallowing bags of food
events.who: René-Antoine Ferchault de Réaumur and Lazzaro Spallanzani
events.text: In 1752 Réaumur got a pet kite, a bird, to swallow little tubes of food and cough them up half-digested. Spallanzani, an Italian priest and scientist, went further and swallowed linen bags and tubes of food himself, then looked at what was left. By 1783 he concluded digestion is chemical, done by juices, not just grinding.
events.why: It turned digestion from guesswork into something you could test.

events.title: A window into a living stomach
events.who: William Beaumont and Alexis St. Martin
events.text: Alexis St. Martin, a French-Canadian fur trader, was shot in the stomach by accident, and the army surgeon William Beaumont saved him. The wound healed with a permanent hole into the stomach. Beaumont dangled food on strings through the hole and drew out digestive juice, and in 1833 published what he learned.
events.why: It proved in a living person that digestion is done by chemical juices, and showed how food leaves the stomach for the intestine.

events.title: The pancreas breaks down fat
events.text: Bernard, a French physiologist, found in 1848 that pancreatic juice turns fat into a milky mix and splits it into smaller pieces. He showed that without this juice, fat is not digested. His famous memoir on the pancreas came out in 1856.
events.why: It showed that the real work of digestion happens in the small intestine, helped by juice from the pancreas.

events.title: A careful picture of coeliac disease
events.text: Gee, a London children's doctor, described children with pale, bulky stools, swollen bellies and poor growth in a paper called On the coeliac affection. He guessed that diet was the key to treating it. He did not yet know which food was to blame.
events.why: It gave the disease a clear modern description, the starting point for finding its cause.

events.title: Watching the gut move by X-ray
events.text: Only months after X-rays were discovered, Cannon, a first-year medical student, fed animals food mixed with bismuth, which shows up on X-rays. He could watch waves of squeezing push food along the gut, and see that fear or distress could stop them. He summed up his work in The Mechanical Factors of Digestion in 1911.
events.why: It was the first time people could watch peristalsis happening inside a living body.

events.title: The law of the intestine
events.text: Bayliss and Starling found that when something stretches the intestine, the muscle just behind it squeezes and the muscle just ahead of it relaxes. This pushes the contents forward. They called it the law of the intestine, and it works even when the gut's links to the brain are cut.
events.why: It explained the reflex behind peristalsis and showed the gut has its own nervous system.

events.title: A chemical message from the gut
events.text: Bayliss and Starling showed that when acid from the stomach reaches the intestine, the gut lining releases a substance into the blood that makes the pancreas pour out its juice. They called it secretin. In 1905 Starling coined the word hormone for chemical messengers like this.
events.why: Secretin is often called the first hormone, and it showed organs can talk to each other through the blood.

events.title: Good bacteria in yogurt
events.text: In 1905 Stamen Grigorov, a young Bulgarian doctor in Geneva, found the rod-shaped bacterium that turns milk into yogurt. Metchnikoff, a Russian-born scientist at the Pasteur Institute, argued in his 1907 book The Prolongation of Life that such bacteria could crowd out harmful gut microbes. He won a Nobel Prize in 1908, for his separate work on immunity.
events.why: It was the start of the idea that some gut bacteria are good for us.

events.title: Wheat is the problem
events.text: Dicke, a Dutch children's doctor, suspected wheat was harming children with coeliac disease. During the hunger winter of 1944 to 1945, when bread was scarce, some of his patients got better, and when bread returned they got worse, according to accounts of his work. In 1950 his thesis showed that removing wheat and some other grains cured the children.
events.why: It gave the world the gluten-free diet.

events.title: Gluten is the harmful part
events.who: Charlotte Anderson, Alastair Frazer and colleagues
events.text: Charlotte Anderson, an Australian doctor, worked with a Birmingham team measuring how well children with coeliac disease absorbed fat. They showed that gluten, a protein in wheat flour, was the part that did the harm. She later became the first woman professor of paediatrics in the UK.
events.why: Pinning the blame on gluten explained why the damaged gut lining could not soak up food.

events.title: Sodium and sugar travel together
events.where: Prague, Czechoslovakia (worked in St. Louis, USA)
events.text: At a meeting in Prague, the American biochemist Robert Crane proposed that gut lining cells pull in glucose and sodium together, through the same doorway. The sodium carries the sugar in with it. Many experts doubted him at first, but he was right.
events.why: It is the reason a drink of salt and sugar can rehydrate a person even when diarrhoea is pouring water out.

events.title: Rehydrating by mouth works
events.who: David Nalin, Richard Cash, Norbert Hirschhorn, Nathaniel Pierce, Rafiqul Islam, A. Majid Molla and others
events.where: Dhaka, then East Pakistan, and Calcutta (Kolkata), India
events.text: Cholera can drain a person of litres of water a day, and the treatment was a drip into a vein. Teams at the Cholera Research Laboratory in Dhaka and the Johns Hopkins centre in Calcutta tested drinks of glucose and salt. In 1968 Nalin and Cash showed that such a drink cut the need for drip fluid by about 80 percent.
events.why: It proved the gut can keep absorbing water during cholera if you give it sugar and salt together.

events.title: The gut's cleaning wave
events.who: Joseph Szurszewski; Gaston Vantrappen and colleagues
events.where: Mayo Clinic, USA, and Leuven, Belgium
events.text: Szurszewski found that between meals, a strong band of squeezing sweeps slowly down a fasting dog's small intestine, again and again. Eating stops it. In 1977 Vantrappen's team found the same pattern in people, and that it was missing in some patients with too many bacteria in the small intestine.
events.why: This migrating motor complex acts as the gut's housekeeper, and may be part of why your tummy rumbles when you are hungry.

events.title: Salt and sugar save a refugee camp
events.text: During the Bangladesh Liberation War, millions fled to India and cholera broke out in the camps. With drips running out, the Kolkata doctor Dilip Mahalanabis and his team gave packets of salt, sugar and baking soda to mix with water, handed out even by people with no medical training. Among about 3,700 patients treated, 3.6 percent died, compared with around 30 percent before.
events.why: It proved oral rehydration works in a real disaster, not just in a hospital.

events.title: The fibre idea
events.text: Burkitt, a surgeon who had worked for years in Uganda, noticed that bowel cancer and other bowel diseases were rare in rural Africa. He gathered reports from well over a thousand rural hospitals in Africa and India. In 1971 he suggested that fibre-rich food, which makes bigger, faster-moving stools, might protect the bowel.
events.why: It started decades of research into how fibre and gut health are linked.

events.title: The most important medical advance of the century?
events.text: In 1978 the medical journal The Lancet wrote that the discovery that glucose helps the gut absorb sodium and water was potentially the most important medical advance of the century. The same year, WHO started its programme to control diarrhoeal diseases. It spread oral rehydration salts around the world with UNICEF.
events.why: It turned a lab discovery into a worldwide life-saving campaign.

events.title: A camera you can swallow
events.who: Gavriel Iddan, Paul Swain and Given Imaging
events.text: Engineers at the Israeli company Given Imaging, working with doctors including Paul Swain in London, built a camera the size of a large pill. It takes photos as the gut squeezes it along and sends them by radio to a recorder. Their paper appeared in Nature in 2000, and the US cleared it for use in 2001.
events.why: For the first time doctors could see the whole small intestine without surgery.

events.title: A better recipe, plus zinc
events.where: Geneva, Switzerland, and New York, USA
events.text: In 2002 WHO released a new oral rehydration formula with less salt and sugar, which the gut absorbs even better. In 2004 WHO and UNICEF advised giving it together with zinc tablets for 10 to 14 days. Zinc shortens bouts of diarrhoea and makes them milder.
events.why: These small changes mean fewer children need a drip or a hospital bed.

events.title: A sari as a cholera filter
events.who: Rita Colwell and colleagues at icddr,b
events.text: Rita Colwell, an American microbiologist, knew cholera bacteria cling to tiny water animals. Her team showed village women how to pour pond and river water through an old sari folded several times. In the villages that filtered their water, cholera cases fell by about half.
events.why: Stopping germs before they reach the gut is as important as treating them after.

events.title: Mapping the microbes in us
events.where: About 80 institutions, mainly in the USA
events.text: The US National Institutes of Health launched the Human Microbiome Project in 2007. Scientists sampled 242 healthy adults at many body sites and read the genes of the microbes they found. In 2012 they published a map of the normal microbes of healthy people, with the gut among the richest places.
events.why: It turned the gut's bacteria from a curiosity into a major field of science.

events.title: Not a tennis court after all
events.text: Textbooks often said the inside of the gut had the area of a tennis court, about 260 to 300 square metres. Helander and Fändriks measured it carefully under the microscope and got about 30 to 40 square metres, about 32 on average. Almost all of it is in the small intestine.
events.why: It fixed a famous wrong number, though the gut's folds, villi and microvilli still make its surface huge.

events.title: Recounting the bacteria
events.who: Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo
events.where: Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot, Israel
events.text: For decades people said bacteria outnumber our own cells ten to one, a rough guess that goes back to a 1972 estimate. Sender, Fuchs and Milo worked it out again and found about 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells in a typical adult. Most of the bacteria live in the large intestine.
events.why: It showed we are roughly half microbe by cell count, not ninety percent.

series.title: Children under 5 dying from diarrhoea each year, worldwide, as estimated at the time
series.caption: Estimates published by WHO and its researchers: deaths fell sharply as oral rehydration spread. Early figures were rough, and the 1980 number rests mostly on surveys from the 1960s and 1970s.

series.title: The same deaths, re-estimated later with modern methods
series.caption: Black et al. (Journal of Global Health, 2019) rebuilt the trend with newer data. They put 1980 lower than the old 4.6 million, but still show a fall of about 80 percent by 2015.

facts: The inside of your gut covers about 32 square metres, roughly the floor of a small studio flat, not the tennis court that old textbooks claimed.
A typical adult carries about 38 trillion bacteria and about 30 trillion human cells, so the famous 'ten bacteria for every human cell' was wrong.
Lazzaro Spallanzani swallowed linen bags full of food and then searched for them afterwards to see what his gut had done.
Alexis St. Martin lived for decades with a hole in his stomach and outlived William Beaumont, the doctor who studied him.
In the 1971 refugee camps, packets of salt, sugar and baking soda cut cholera deaths from about 30 in every 100 patients to under 4.
